1:
Ellicott hears a new train of imagery beginning, linked to the previous chapter by the word tabernacle and perhaps suggested by Paul's own trade. His daily work was a parable to him: while his hands ran up temporary shelter for men travelling on earth, he thought of the house not made with hands. The comparison of the body to a dwelling was common enough — Ellicott notes it in the Greek medical writers — but the substitution of a tent for a house makes the point transitory. Gill develops the figure both ways. The body is a house because it is a curious piece of architecture, its parts fitly framed in just proportion, which argues the wisdom of the architect; and because it is the soul's dwelling, which shows the soul more excellent than the body, independent of it, and capable of a separate existence. It is earthly because it comes from the earth, is supported by earthly things, and will quickly return there; and a tabernacle by allusion to the tents of soldiers, shepherds and travellers, soon set up and soon struck. Robertson confirms the picture from the grammar: the genitive is appositive, so the house simply is the tent, and the verb for dissolving is the very word used for taking a tent down. Wesley adds only that it was never designed for a lasting habitation.

What the promised building is remains open. Barnes reports Robinson's view that it means the future spiritual body, notes that others have supposed a celestial vehicle with which God clothes the soul in the intermediate state, and objects that Scripture is silent about any such vehicle. Clarke is one of those others, and he reaches the idea by a careful reading of the Mosaic tabernacle: when the congregation moved, the tent was taken to pieces, the ark carried separately under its own covering, and the whole re-erected at the place of rest. So the body is dissolved in order to be built again; the soul subsists apart as the ark did; and as the ark had its own veil, the soul must have some vehicle to subsist in until it receives its body at the resurrection. Calvin declines to choose between a state of blessed immortality after death and the incorruptible body after the resurrection, saying either sense suits — though he prefers to make the first the commencement of the thing and the second its consummation, which he thinks fits the argument better. Robertson observes that the possession is present: we have, indicative, holding the title now by faith, faith being the title-deed to things hoped for.

Most weight falls on the opening verb. Calvin insists the knowledge does not spring from human intellect but from the revelation of the Spirit, and is therefore peculiar to believers. The heathen had some notion of the soul's immortality, but none could claim assurance of it: Cicero argues the case at length and seemingly beyond answer, then introduces a speaker complaining that while he reads he assents, and the moment he lays the book down the assent is gone. Seneca, reviewing the same philosophers, remarked that immortality was rather promised than proved by those great men. Calvin adds that the knowledge must be particular and not general, since a persuasion that God's children fare better after death, without assurance for oneself, would console nobody. Barnes agrees the phrase is the language of unwavering assurance, and takes it as proof that such assurance is attainable. Henry distinguishes the two things it covers — the truth of a future blessedness, and a good hope through grace of one's own interest in it. Chrysostom draws the practical conclusion hardest: since the destruction of the outward man conducts us to immortality, one ought not merely to avoid grieving at its partial decay, but earnestly to seek that the destruction be completed.
2:
The figure shifts without warning from a dwelling to a garment, and everyone notices. Barnes calls it an evident change of metaphor that gives the construction an apparent harshness, and observes that both figures were common in antiquity — the Pythagoreans comparing the body to a tent or hut, the Platonists to a vestment. Robertson enjoys the collision rather than apologising for it, noting that the verb is a double compound meaning to put on over oneself, and that the result is a mixed metaphor: putting on a dwelling-place as if it were clothing. Ellicott thinks the transition natural enough, since each of the two shelters a man and each is separable from the man himself, so that both answer to the body which invests the spirit. Wesley supplies the substance of the hope in one line — instead of flesh and blood, which cannot enter heaven, the rising body will be covered with what answers to them but is incorruptible and immortal. Ellicott alone hears something more personal in the groaning. Taken with what the letter has already said, he cannot read it as merely a strong way of expressing the weariness of life, and finds in it the pressure of an actual illness.

Clarke and Barnes work from the same rabbinic source and reach opposite verdicts on its value. Clarke holds that the expressions are Jewish and can only be interpreted as the Jews used them, and sets out the usage at length. The Hebrew verb for clothing means to be surrounded or invested with anything, so that a man may be said to be clothed with the cloud, or the righteous with a crown of light. The Hebrew word for house frequently denotes a case or cover — the house of the face is a veil, the house of the fingers gloves, the house of the feet shoes — so that being clothed on with a house may signify a settled quality of the soul, in the way we ourselves speak of a habit of vice or of virtue. He adds that the Jews assign garments to the soul in both worlds, hold that its clothing is the image of God which Adam lost, and describe the angel of death as removing the mortal garment and putting on one from paradise. Barnes knows the same collection of sayings and refuses it flatly: there is no reason to think Paul referred to any such trifles, since he plainly regarded man as body and soul, the body being the soul's dwelling.

On not being found naked, Barnes lists five renderings — Locke's, Rosenmüller's, Tindale's, Doddridge's and Hammond's — and then gives his own: the clause means that in the future state the soul will not be destitute of a body, but clothed in its appropriate glorified one, so that the union of body and soul will be known there as here. Ellicott says the Greek particles assert more than the English concedes, and would paraphrase them "if, as I believe"; the point being that to a Greek the world of the dead was a place of shadows, whereas Paul is certain that in the state of glory nothing will be shadowy or unreal. Robertson defines the word by Plummer's phrase for it, disembodied spirits without form and void of all power of activity. Calvin dissents from Chrysostom and others who find nothing new in the clause, and reads a twofold clothing instead: the righteousness of Christ and the sanctification of the Spirit now, immortality and glory afterwards — those whom God means to glorify he first justifies. Gill refers the supposition to the saints alive at Christ's coming, who will never be stripped of the body at all, and Clarke asks only that a man be so prepared here as not to be found destitute of the divine image there.
4:
Robertson insists the negative has been put in the wrong place. The sense is not that we would rather not be unclothed, but that we do not wish to take the clothing off at all — we wish to put more on; Paul has no desire to be a bare disembodied spirit without his spiritual garment. He borrows Plummer's formula for what survives: only what is mortal perishes, while the personality, made of soul and body together, goes on. Ellicott reads the same wish as the expectation of a man who thought the Coming near, hoping to remain until it and to let the incorruptible supervene upon the corruptible, so as to be changed rather than to die. Calvin, who takes the words more generally, is the frankest about the reluctance behind them. He grants that we have a natural aversion to quitting this life considered in itself, as no one willingly lets himself be stripped of his clothes; but the natural horror of death is overcome by confidence, in the way a man parts without reluctance from a coarse, dirty, threadbare and tattered garment when an elegant and durable one is waiting for him. That, he says, is what it means for the mortal to be swallowed up of life.

Barnes is anxious that the motive not be mistaken. The groaning is not impatience, and the mere fact that a man may be afflicted much and long should never be the principal reason for wishing to depart; Paul was willing to bear trials as long as God appointed, and his desire to be gone rose from something higher than a wish to escape trouble. Clarke says the same in his own key — we do not desire death, even with eternal glory in full prospect, an hour before the time God has assigned, and would not die, whatever tribulation we pass through, until the whole will of God is accomplished in us and by us. Wesley notes how exactly the words are chosen, since a burden naturally produces a groan, and adds that faith does not share the philosophical contempt for what the wise Creator has given. Gill measures the groaning by who is exempt from it: the saints no longer in the tabernacle have done groaning, their bodies in the grave and their souls at rest, delivered from every oppressor; it is those still in the unsettled state who groan, in the midst of tribulation and not yet in the happiness they are wishing for.

The next verse traces the longing itself back to God, and Ellicott presses the argument furthest. The very thing we were wrought for is the consummation in which mortality is swallowed up of life; redemption, the new birth and the gifts of the Spirit were all looking toward that result. He draws a striking inference from the kind of gift given: every spiritual energy that does not depend on the material organism is evidence that the organism is an impediment to the Spirit's free action, our eyes being limits to perception as well as instruments of it. Clarke takes the same verse to mean that God has given us an insatiable hungering after righteousness and immortality, and quotes Addison's lines on it — whence this pleasing hope, this fond desire, this longing after immortality? — answering that it is the divinity that stirs within us. Calvin agrees the disposition is supernatural, since natural feeling never reaches it, and finds the Spirit's office here in showing believers what they ought to desire. Gill rests on the maker: God's counsels are immutable, and whatever he begins he finishes. Cyril of Jerusalem cites the verse for a different purpose, among his proofs that Paul and his fellow apostles were full of the Holy Spirit.
6:
The two verbs Paul uses are a matched pair, and the grammarians make the most of them. Robertson notes that both are rare, formed from words for a man among his own people and a man away from home, and that the papyri show the same contrast; Ellicott adds that neither occurs elsewhere in the New Testament, and that the construction is participial, the sentence broken off and started again two verses later. Barnes reports a dispute over the first. Doddridge would render it "sojourning in the body," objecting that "at home in the body" contradicts the very point Paul is making, since this is precisely not our home; Bloomfield answers that the word never bears the sense of sojourning. Barnes takes the plain course of translating it simply as being in the body, and is more interested in the adjective at the head of the verse: the word means to be of good cheer, and Tindale so rendered it. What he wants noticed is that Paul says always. The cheerfulness was not occasional or passing but constant, which he takes as an instance of what an assured prospect of heaven does — it lets a man face danger with courage and endure toil with patience.

Calvin raises the difficulty the verse creates. Scripture everywhere proclaims that God is with us; Paul here says we are away from him. He resolves it by distinguishing the senses: God is with all men in upholding them by his power, and with his believing people by the energy of his Spirit, residing among them; yet he is absent in that he does not present himself to be seen face to face, we being still in exile from his kingdom. The absence, he insists, is one of knowledge only. He adds the contrast that gives the verse its force: unbelievers are in a perpetual ferment of anxiety, or else murmur against God, because they expect shortly to cease existing and have set the summit of their happiness in this life. Clarke works the same ground and turns it into a polemic. Heaven is the Christian's home, and while the body is the soul's proper lodging here, the soul was made for glory and that glory is its country; nor is it heaven merely that is in view but the Lord, without whom heaven would be no rest at all. He then observes that Paul leaves no room, between being in the body and being with the Lord, for any sleep of the soul. Wesley says only that we behave undauntedly, most of all with death in view.

The famous clause turns out to be mistranslated, and Ellicott says so with visible regret. The word rendered "sight" never means the faculty of seeing but always the form and fashion of the thing seen, so the sense is by faith and not by appearance; it seems almost a pity, he admits, to alter so familiar and favourite a text. Robertson gives the same correction in three words, and Calvin had made it already, noting that the term is ambiguous. Barnes is content with the traditional wording and presses the practical sense instead: to walk is to live and conduct oneself, and the Christian orders his life by things unseen as the world orders its life by things seen. He turns the objection back on the objector: all men act on what they have not seen, hoping for what is future, aspiring to happiness they have never beheld, striving for wealth still at a distance. Gill grants that there is something of sight in faith, but seeing through a glass darkly rather than face to face; Wesley says the same — the evidence faith gives implies a kind of seeing him who is invisible, yet is as far beneath what we shall have as it is above unassisted reason.
8:
The preference stated here looks like a reversal of the one stated a few verses earlier, and Ellicott takes the difficulty seriously. Paul had said he did not wish to put the garment off; now he says he would rather be out of the body. The expression here, Ellicott answers, is weaker: we are content, if death comes before the Lord's coming, to accept it, since even without the glory of the resurrection body it makes us at home with Christ. If a shadow of inconsistency remains, he takes it as the natural outcome of a man in a strait between two. He then offers a second and bolder reading. Paul elsewhere describes visions of which he could not say whether they were in the body or out of it; perhaps he means that even here he takes pleasure in the state which seems to carry him out of the body, since in it his eyes are opened on the unseen. Both verbs stand in a tense of single action rather than continuous state, which he thinks tells for this. Robertson renders the verb "we are well-pleased, we prefer," if left to ourselves, and marks the following infinitive as ingressive: to reach that goal is bliss. Clarke keeps the balance — we prefer glory to suffering, yet as Christians cannot wish to die before our time — and Gill notes the cheerfulness that goes with the assurance.

Barnes reads the clause as evidence and enumerates what it excludes. Since to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord, the departed spirits of the saints are with the Redeemer at once: not annihilated; not sleeping in an unconscious state, as Priestley supposed; not in an intermediate place, whether the purgatory of the Papists or the common abode of just and unjust that many Protestants have imagined. He adds that for Paul the Lord Jesus is the glory of heaven, and that he had no conception of a heaven where Christ was not. Calvin draws the same inference and presses further into the affections: true faith produces not merely contempt of death but a desire for it, so that when dread of death outweighs the joy of hope, that is a token of unbelief. He is careful to add the limit — believers do not by importunate desire try to anticipate their Lord's day, but willingly keep their footing here as long as he sees good. Wesley states the doctrinal result in one line, that the happiness of the saints is not deferred to the resurrection.

"We labour" understates the next verb, and three of them say so. The word is built from love and honour, and Ellicott would render it: our ambition is that we may be well-pleasing to him — noting that the adjective names the quality on which acceptance depends rather than the act of accepting. Robertson calls it ambition in the good sense, remarking that the nearest Latin word carries a bad one, and that the adjective turns up in inscriptions of the period. Clarke takes it as acting at all times on principles of honour, and since Christians claim kindred with the inhabitants of heaven, acting as they do; he adds that this is itself the substance of heaven, to study to love and please and serve the one from whom we have received our being and its blessings. Calvin explains why the exhortation is needed. Hope of resurrection and thought of judgment naturally awaken this desire, and the reason we are indolent is that we seldom remember we are lodgers here for a short time. He notes too that the desire is ascribed to the present and the absent alike, which confirms once more that the soul survives. Henry states the corollary bluntly: well-grounded hopes of heaven do not encourage sloth or sinful security.
10:
Ellicott objects to the English before he reaches the doctrine. "Appear" should be "be made manifest," the same word rendered "make manifest the counsels of the heart" earlier in the correspondence and used again in the very next verse; varying it, he says, was done only from the translators' desire to vary, and it hides both the echo and the connection. On the noun he supplies the setting. The word is not the throne of the Gospels but the raised tribunal of a Roman magistrate, standing at the end of the hall above the floor — a term that in classical Greek meant the orator's platform rather than the judge's chair, and that passed later to the bishop's seat when basilicas became churches. Robertson gives its derivation from a word for a step, and marks the pronoun: Christ is Saviour, Lord and Judge of us all, the all. Gill fills in what the day will look like — the awfulness of the summons to the dead to rise and come to judgment, the sudden and glorious appearing of the Judge, the placing of the thrones, the opening of the books, the sentence and its immediate execution — and observes that ministers know the Judge and know the day is fixed, though not when.

The clause about receiving according to what one has done provokes the sharpest exchange in the chapter. Ellicott calls it an unqualified assertion of the universal law of retribution, and says it would seem impossible to evade its force but for the perverse ingenuity of the system-builders of theology: no formula of justification by faith, imputed righteousness, pardon sealed in blood or priestly absolution is allowed to mingle with what Paul expects of that day. Calvin, one of the builders complained of, had already answered the objection in his own terms. Evil deeds, he says, are requited with the punishment they deserve; but in rewarding good deeds God does not look to merit, since no work is so complete in all its parts as to be deservedly pleasing to him. The only resource is that he accepts us of unmerited goodness and justifies us by not imputing our sins, and having received us into favour he then receives our works also by a gracious acceptance. On that footing there is no inconsistency in saying he rewards good works, provided we grant that eternal life is obtained gratuitously. Wesley adds a gentler note on what will be uncovered — even sins long since forgiven, but disclosed at the man's own desire, without grief and without shame.

"Terror" is a mistranslation, and Clarke is angriest about it. The phrase means the fear of the Lord, which in Scripture often stands for the reverence owed to him; and men who justify constant declamation on hell and perdition by quoting this text, he says, know little of its meaning and less of the spirit of the gospel — let them learn from Christ weeping over Jerusalem, and from his prayer for those who crucified him. Where terror reigns, he adds, there can be neither fear nor faith nor love, nor hope either. Barnes, who keeps the older word, arrives at the same place by attending to the verb: Paul does not say we drive men, or frighten them, but we persuade them, and constant appeal to fear was not the method of either the apostle or the Saviour. Chrysostom sees a further strictness in the ministry it produced — not merely refusing to give any handle of offence, but declining to repel a false suspicion when it could have been repelled. Calvin sums up what such a life rests on: as my mouth speaks to men, so does my heart to God. Boasting is empty where the evidence is missing, since none are bolder in claiming everything than those who have nothing.
12:
Ellicott hears the sentence as a flinch. Paul has barely finished appealing to their consciences when the old sneer stings him again — so he is commending himself once more — and this is his answer to it: not commendation, but the giving of a starting-point for a boast he assumes the body of the church will be glad to make on his behalf. The better manuscripts, he adds, omit the opening "For," and the sense runs better without it. Barnes reads the same defensive purpose and spells out its logic: they were converted under Paul's labours and regard him as their father in the gospel, yet they hear him slandered as no true apostle, so he furnishes them with the materials of a reply, and in vindicating him they vindicate their own attachment. Calvin turns it into a rule about reputation. A servant of Christ should care for his own good name only so far as it serves the church; and he detects a reproach in the words, since the Corinthians ought to have magnified Paul's apostleship of their own accord instead of forcing him to do it, it being their interest rather than his that it should be held in honour.

Who the men glorying in appearance were is guessed at from the phrase. Clarke supposes a particular false apostle who had been dividing the church and building a party round himself; Robertson names the Judaizers, braggarts about their orthodox Judaism. Ellicott offers a more concrete and less flattering suggestion. The words might cover anything external — claims of authority, of training, of knowledge — but the way Paul uses the term later in the letter points to something narrower: men were contrasting the imposing presence of his rivals with his own bodily weakness and small stature. Take your stand against that boast, he is telling the Corinthians, on the work done in your consciences. Robertson glosses the noun Paul uses for what he gives them as a base of operations, material to work from — as we might say a tip, only far more. Henry states the principle underneath: when the ministry of the word is vilified, the best defence its people can offer is that the word has been manifested to their own consciences and been effectual to their conversion and building up.

The charge behind the next verse is derangement, and Gill recalls that Festus made it to Paul's face. Barnes takes the accusation as perennial rather than local: it has never been uncommon for the cold and the prudent, for formal professors and for hypocrites, to reckon the warm-hearted friends of religion maniacs, and the same thing was said of the Saviour by his own relatives. He is careful about what follows from this. Being unlike other men does not prove a man deranged, but neither, he grants, does zeal excuse extravagance; what Paul appeals to is the principle actually moving him. Calvin treats the clause as a concession made in the language of the objectors, since Paul's glorying was in fact sane — a sober and most judicious madness, if the phrase may be allowed. What the concession secures is indifference: he is content to be reckoned mad or sober as men please, being as ready to be silent as to speak, so long as God is served and the church advantaged. Wesley draws the pastoral consequence, that congregations generally prefer the calmer manner in their teachers, but that teachers must obey God whoever is offended by it.
14:
Whose love is meant, Christ's for us or ours for him? Barnes admits the phrase will bear either, that expositors differ, and that nothing but the run of the argument can decide; he settles for Christ's love toward us, since it is the dying that supplies the motive. Ellicott calls Paul's uniform use of this and like phrases elsewhere decisive for the same view, and Robertson simply labels the genitive subjective. Wesley declines to choose, taking it of Christ's love to us and ours to him together, and holding that it constrains us to both. On the verb they agree better. Gill prefers "containeth us," holding us to our station as soldiers are held together under a banner displayed, and remembers that the church once said his banner over her was love. Barnes traces the word from holding together and pressing together to urging and impelling; Robertson finds the same range in it — pressing the ears shut, pressing on every side, holding fast — and concludes that Paul's sense of Christ's love holds him together to his task whatever men think or say. Wesley supplies the image the others lack, of winds and tides bearing a vessel on with a strong, steady, prevailing influence to its destined harbour.

"Then were all dead" is the crux, and the readings diverge sharply. Clarke takes the first clause as granted — that Christ died for all mankind, which he says no primitive Christian ever did or could doubt — and infers the second from it: had all not been guilty and consigned to death for their sins, there could have been no need of his dying. Wesley reasons the same way, that all, even the best of men, are naturally in a state of spiritual death, since had any man been otherwise Christ need not have died for him. Ellicott sets this aside on grammatical grounds. The verb stands in the tense of a momentary act of dying, not of a state of death, so the words cannot mean that all were previously under sentence, nor that all were dead in trespasses and sins; nor can they well mean that all paid the penalty vicariously, since the stress of the context falls not on the claims of justice but on union with Christ. Robertson reads it as Ellicott's grammar requires and Clarke's theology allows: the one died for the all, and so the all died when he did. The preposition, he adds, is the ordinary Greek word for substitution, common in that sense in the papyri.

The purpose clause draws a distinction Barnes is careful to press. Paul does not say that all for whom Christ died now live, but that those who live should not live to themselves; and that difference, Barnes argues, shows there may be many for whom he died who are never made alive to God. The very breadth of the benevolence then becomes the argument: those who have in fact been benefited by so unbounded a love owe it their whole service. Calvin reaches the same obligation from the side of ownership. Christ redeemed us that he might hold us as his own possession, so that we are no longer our own masters; and he separates the two things the passage asks — that we should be dead in Christ, laying aside all ambition and eagerness for distinction until it is no hardship to be made nothing, and that we should owe him our living and our dying alike. Ellicott adds a caution against overreading: Paul was not writing a theological treatise, and this is no exhaustive account of the purposes of Christ's death, but gives prominence to one — that men should share his death and his life at once. Wesley names what living to oneself means, the seeking of one's own honour, profit and pleasure.
16:
To know a man after the flesh is to take his measure by what the world can see, and the commentators itemise the discarded standards. Gill lists carnal descent and the privileges of Jewish birth, outward condition among the rich and honourable, and natural parts — learning, wisdom, eloquence. Barnes reduces the verb to forming an estimate, and names three things that no longer weighed with Paul: birth and country, so that he was drawn neither to a Jew for being a Jew nor to a Gentile for being one; rank, wealth and office, which had weighed with him before his conversion; and the claims of his own kindred, whom he had left in order to preach. Clarke reaches the same result from the other end — since all alike are shut up in unbelief and children of wrath, there is nothing in family or stock to esteem. Wesley draws the sharpest edge on it. We fear not the great, he writes; we regard not the rich or wise; we account not the least less than ourselves; we consider all, only in order to save all. Then he turns the description into a question, and asks who it is that knows no one after the flesh, and in what land such Christians live.

The parenthesis about having known Christ after the flesh is harder, and Ellicott puts two questions to it. What provoked it? Probably a party at Corinth claiming a special relation to Christ as personal disciples, perhaps pressing the claims of his brother according to the flesh; judging him so would be, for Paul, to judge him by the world's standard. And what does the admission mean? Not, he thinks, that Paul had seen Jesus of Nazareth and misjudged him, but that he had once expected the Messiah as others did, with the hopes of an earthly kingdom restored. Robertson agrees the concession is real and locates it in Paul's pre-conversion judgement of Christ by the standards of the Sanhedrin, adding that whether Paul ever saw Jesus in the flesh is a question on which this verse says nothing. Henry leaves the same question open but presses the doctrine: the bodily presence of Christ is not to be desired or doted on by his disciples, and those who make images of him for worship have not taken the way God appointed for strengthening faith. Calvin warns against a further abuse, noting that Servetus made the verse prove that Christ's humanity is now swallowed up in his divinity, whereas Paul speaks of outward appearance and not of the substance of his body.

Whether the last clause states a fact or issues a command divides them. Calvin supplies an ellipsis and reads a demand — whoever wishes to hold a place in the kingdom of Christ, let him be a new creature — and uses it to condemn every excellence, learning and eloquence included, where renovation of heart is wanting. Barnes knows the reading and rejects it, calling this one of the places where the margin is less correct than the text: the point is not that a Christian ought to be a new creation but that he is one, and will in fact live like it. Clarke presses the strength of the phrase. The man is not merely mended but new made, a new creation and a little world in himself, where formerly all was chaotic disorder; and he notes that the Jews called a convert's turning a new creation, one rabbi holding that whoever converts a man has as good as created him. Wesley says the same in his own compass — only the power that makes a world can make a Christian — and describes new senses, new faculties, new affections, so that the man lives as it were in a new world, the old things falling away of their own accord, like snow in spring.
18:
"All things" is narrower than it looks. Ellicott points to the article in the Greek: Paul is speaking not of the universe at large but of the new things belonging to the new creation just named. Gill fills in what those things are — the bringing of men into a gospel church state, the abrogation of the ceremonial law and its sacrifices, the ejection of Satan from the heathen temples, the passing away of everything the old order held. Ellicott adds a chronological note of some interest, that this is the earliest place in Paul's letters where the word for reconciling describes God's work in Christ, and that in that sense it occurs only here and in the epistle written soon afterwards. Robertson supplies the word's history — it was the ordinary term for exchanging coins — and then states the point that governs everything following: God needs no reconciliation, but is engaged in the business of reconciling us to himself. Clarke locates the obstacle accordingly. There is an enmity in the heart of man against sacred things, and it is that enmity, not any reluctance on God's side, which is the grand hindrance to his salvation; the word itself, he notes, means to change thoroughly.

How the famous clause should be construed is disputed. Barnes allows two senses — that God acted by means of Christ, or, with Doddridge, that God was united to Christ and manifested himself in him. Calvin insists on the fuller reading and identifies the subject: it is of the Father that this is said, since it would be improper to speak of Christ's divine nature as being in Christ. He then gives the sentence its weight — God had withdrawn to a distance from us, and in Christ he has drawn near, so that Christ is the true Emmanuel and his coming is God's own approach to men. Ellicott prefers a different arrangement again, taking both nouns as anarthrous and rendering it: how that it was God who was reconciling in Christ a world unto himself. He concedes that the received construction is grammatically tenable and that every English version from Wiclif onward has adopted it, noting only that Tyndale, Cranmer and the Geneva translators rendered the verb as making agreement between the world and himself. Wesley identifies the subject as the whole Godhead, though more eminently the Father, and Robertson observes that the connecting idiom, unclassical though it is, turns up in the papyri and means something like "how that."

On the non-imputing of trespasses Barnes fastens on which party moved first. Man had no plan for reconciliation and no desire for it; it was the offended party, not the offending, who sought terms, and that measures the strength of the love. God did not charge their offences home with inexorable severity, but provided a pardon and offered to remit sin on the conditions of the gospel. Ellicott counts the vocabulary — the verb for reckoning is peculiarly prominent just then, occurring eight times in this letter and nineteen in the epistle written next — and refuses to be troubled by the obvious objection. The difficulty of squaring a God who does not reckon trespasses with the judgment according to works, which he had asserted just as flatly earlier in the chapter, did not present itself to the apostle's mind, and need not present itself to ours. Calvin faces the same tension from the other side, holding that men return into favour precisely by being reckoned righteous through the remission of sins, since while God imputes sin he must regard the sinner with abhorrence — and then admits the further difficulty, that Scripture also says we were loved before the world was made.
20:
The word for ambassador carries a history, and three of them trace it. Barnes derives the verb from the word for an old man or elder, notes Tindale's "messengers in the room of Christ," and borrows Webster's definition of a minister of the highest rank sent by one prince to the court of another; in every country and age, he adds, the person of an ambassador has been held inviolable. Robertson supplies the contemporary usage: it was the proper term in the Greek East for the Emperor's legate, and appears as such in inscriptions and papyri, so that Paul may be allowed a natural pride in claiming it. He notes too the condition of the office, that the man must be acceptable at both courts, the one he represents and the one he is sent to. Ellicott turns to the English instead. The earlier versions gave "messengers" and the Rhemish "legates"; "ambassadors," which he calls singularly felicitous, first appears in the version of 1611, the word having reached English through the Romance languages and become current, he suspects, through Elizabethan dealings with France and Spain. Clarke states the chain of representation plainly: Christ on earth represented the Sovereign of the world, and his apostles represent Christ.

What the envoy is authorised to say divides Gill from the rest. Barnes takes the ministers' business to be explaining and enforcing the terms on which God is willing to be reconciled, forbidding them only to negotiate on new terms, to alter what God has proposed, or to follow plans of their own. Gill will not allow even that much latitude: they come with full powers, he says, not to propose terms of peace nor to treat with men about it, but to publish and proclaim a peace already made. Calvin is occupied with a prior question, how such a message can be trusted at all. Nobody would rest his eternal salvation on the promise of a man, so the messengers must be known to be ordained by God and God must be understood to speak through them — which is why Christ said that hearing them is hearing him. From this he draws a hard conclusion about the hierarchy of his own day, that men who do not discharge this embassy are neither apostles nor pastors, whatever they are called, but dumb idols. Robertson reduces the message itself to its grammatical force: the verb is an imperative of a single act, so the sense is get reconciled to God, and do it now.

The astonishing thing is the beseeching, and Wesley puts it as a pair of questions: did a judge ever beseech a condemned criminal to accept a pardon, or a creditor beseech a ruined debtor to receive an acquittance in full? Yet the eternal Judge not only offers these blessings but invites, entreats, and solicits with the most tender importunity that they be not rejected. Calvin finds the same wonder in the single word, that Christ stoops so low as not to disdain to beg of us, and adds that the embassy is a continuing one — Christ did not suffer merely to expiate sins once, nor is the gospel meant only for offences committed before baptism, but as we sin daily we are daily received back by remission. Ellicott closes the argument by marking what Paul does not say. He recognises the representative and vicarious character of the work fully, yet stands clear of the speculative systems built on his words: there is here no wrath of the Father averted by the compassion of the Son, nor any penalty exacted as a quantitative equivalent for the sins of men. The whole originates in the Father's love, and he does not need to be reconciled. How the death was effective remains, on Butler's phrase, mysterious and in part unrevealed.
21:
Before the paradox comes the claim of sinlessness, and it is pressed hard. Robertson reads the participle as a definite assertion that Jesus never committed sin and had no personal acquaintance with it, quoting Bernard's phrase that Christ was and is a moral miracle, and therefore more than merely man. Ellicott draws the distinction that gives the claim its edge: every other man has learned what sin can do by yielding to it, while Christ alone learned it by resisting and yet suffering its effects. Clarke reaches the same sense through the idiom, noting that not to know sin is the same as being conscious of innocence, and citing the Latin commonplace that to be conscious of no fault is to have nothing to turn pale at. Gill is careful to state how far the sinlessness reached and where it stopped. Christ took flesh of a sinful woman, though what he took was not sinful, being sanctified by the Spirit who formed his human nature; he appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, attended by the infirmities that are the effects of sin, and was traduced by men as a sinner. Wesley calls the description a commendation peculiar to Christ.

"Made him to be sin" is the hardest phrase in the chapter and the commentators divide sharply over it. Clarke argues that the noun means a sin-offering, the Septuagint using it in more than ninety places for the offering, and charges the English translators with inconsistency: had they rendered it here as they do in Leviticus, they would not have given a false view of a passage made the foundation of what he calls a blasphemous doctrine — that our sins were imputed to Christ so that he became a proper object of divine indignation, some writers going so far as to call him the greatest of sinners. Gill holds the doctrine Clarke attacks, in its strongest form: besides being made a sacrifice, Christ was made sin itself by imputation, and treated by God's justice as though he were not merely a sinner but a mass of sin, since to be made sin says more than to be made a sinner. Ellicott rejects the sin-offering reading outright, calling that sense foreign to the New Testament and doubtful even in the Old, and holds instead that God dealt with Christ as though he were sin, absolutely identified with it. Barnes accepts the offering sense while ruling out three things: Christ was not sin in the abstract, not a sinner, and not guilty in any proper sense, since guilt belongs only to a personal transgressor and a guilty being's sufferings could carry no merit.

Calvin makes the two halves of the verse measure each other: we are righteous in God's sight in the same respect in which Christ was a sinner, since he took our place to be dealt with as a criminal in our room, not for his own offences but for others', and so his condemnation was our absolution. Ellicott presses the phrase "the righteousness of God" further than either imputation or requirement. It names the attribute that belongs to God himself, and by identification with Christ — first objectively, so far as God's action is concerned, and then by that act of will which Paul calls faith — men are made sharers in it. On his reading the point of the verse is that the purpose of the death was not only or chiefly that men should escape punishment, but that they should become righteous; and he notes that Paul, having supplied the germ from which forensic theories of the atonement have been developed, does not develop one himself. Wesley combines the two accounts, taking the righteousness as first imputed and then implanted. Robertson lets the verb settle it, underlining that Paul writes not that we may be reckoned but that we may become.
